newsitem.title: USA: Dollar battered by comments of foreign, U.S. officials.
newsitem.headline: Dollar battered by comments of foreign, U.S. officials.

text.p: NEW YORK, Nov 7 - The dollar tumbled against the yen Thursday to its lowest level in nearly a month, buffeted by comments from a senior Japanese offical and the head of a manufacturers group in the United States.

The Nikkei Financial Daily newspaper quoted Eisuke Sakakibara as saying the dollar's correction from last year's sharp slide against the yen was about finished and that Japan's Ministry of Finance was not trying to weaken the yen further.

When questioned by reporters later, Sakakibara, director-general of the International Finance Bureau, stood by his remarks. He also said the financial markets' view of the Japanese economy was too pessimistic and that the economy was stronger than the markets' assessment.

This was echoed by the director-general of Japan's Economic Planning Agency, Taro Aso, who conceded the economic recovery is still moderate but emphasised that conditions have improved from two or three months ago.

"The Japanese government feels that the yen does not need to weaken any further and that the economy is a little stronger than it's been given credit for," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc., a consulting firm. He predicted the dollar's decline against the yen is not finished.

The Bank of Japan has kept official interest rates at rock-bottom levels to help stimulate economic growth in Japan, but rates may increase as the economy rebounds. Higher rates would help the Japanese currency by making yen-denominated deposits more attractive to foreign investors.
The dollar began slipping in Tokyo and slid even further when trading got underway in Europe and New York.
The U.S. currency fell in New York to 111.27 yen, its lowest level since reaching 110.85 yen on Oct. 11. It also weakened against other major currencies.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 111.90 yen and 1.5112 German marks, down from 113.95 yen and 1.5175 marks on Wednesday.

Remarks by Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, added to the dollar's woes. He predicted the White House will de-emphasise the value of a strong dollar as the U.S. economy slows.
Such a change would contrast with the policy adopted by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who has repeatedly called for a strong dollar.
A firm dollar can hurt foreign demand for American-made exports, but it may help by making U.S. stocks and bonds more attractive to foreign investors.
Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank, doubted that Rubin would endorse a weak dollar policy.
"I think he would recognise that the dollar strength is very important to the U.S. economy drawing investment from overseas," Dix said.

In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.2734 Swiss francs late Thursday from 1.2775 francs on Wednesday. The British pound climbed to $1.6490 from $1.6415. The dollar slid to Canadian $1.3292 from C1.3318.
